blocks.text: These we have rendered in Latin words almost word for word thus: [col. 195]
Grey-eyed, and with eyes that never deceive, What the hunter does not see, that bird sees.

We have said that these words bear especially on our subject, because the following is read of the eye of this same bird, Iob. XXVIII, 7: The bird עיט knew not the path, nor has עין איה, the eye of the aja, seen it. He is speaking of mines, from which metals are dug out by human industry. Since these lie hidden in the innermost bowels of the earth, their path, [II, 782] says the sacred writer, the עיט ajit knew not, that is, not just any bird, but the bird of prey, a kind that is far more keen-sighted. This is in the first hemistich; and in the other, parallel to it: Nor has the eye of the aja, or juju if you prefer, seen it, that is, of the smerillon [merlin], although that bird is most sharp-eyed and sees as keenly as the eagle or the Epidaurian serpent. Many things prove that the smerillon is the αἰσαλών [aisalōn], the aesalon, of the ancients. 1. Aristotle (Hist. book 9, ch. 36) and Pliny (book 10, ch. 8) list the aesalon among the species of hawks. 2. By Aelian (book 2, ch. 51) it is called ὄρνις ἰσχυρός [ornis ischyros] ^{(3)}. 3. And by Pliny (book 10, ch. 74) a small bird. 4. The same Pliny (book 10, ch. 8) writes that the aesalon appears at every season, whereas the others depart in winter. This fits the smerillon exactly, as Turner has noted. His words are: Among the smaller hawks only the merlin, as the English call it, or smerla, as the Germans do, is always seen. Yet the most noble Lord de Grentemesnil contends that this is false. Some write aesaron instead of aesalon. Hesychius: Αἰσάρων· εἶδος ἱέρακος [Aisarōn; eidos hierakos]. Both perhaps come from αἶσα [aisa], because it is a bird αἴσιος [aisios], auspicious and of good omen, like every kind of hawk. This I could prove without any trouble, if it were worth the effort.
